"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 192: a weak, unstructured readout of the MLP.

What it is: a single rank-one piece of layer 15's down projection. Its activation is a
fixed linear readout of the MLP hidden state (about 42% of it is one hidden unit, 192).
That unit's sign and size depend on the wider context, not on the current token: token
identity, previous token, token class, position and repetition each explain under 1% of
the variance, and the best document-level average explains about 7%.

What the program does: the one regularity found is that the activation is ~0 on a
document's first token (measured mean 0.0015, all 1536 sampled instances within 0.003 of 0).
Elsewhere it predicts the component's average value over ordinary tokens, about 0.06.
This is the best mean-squared prediction the readable features tried here reach; it
explains essentially none of the variance (about 0).
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.06  # average over ordinary (non-first) tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    starts_document = t == 0 or ids[t] != ids[t - 1]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""MLP hidden unit 193 of layer 15 (the down_proj component 193).

What it responds to: this unit's output promotes words such as "expensive", "costly",
"unavailable" and "difficult". It is positive where the text describes something as hard,
costly, scarce or limited ("more expensive", "harder to learn", "not readily available"),
and on contrastive connectives ("However", "But") that set up such a point. It is negative
in an assistant's refusals and apologies ("I cannot", "I am not able", "unfortunately", "sorry").

The program reads only the current token and predicts from three word lists, with weights
rounded from a least-squares fit on a sample of the training data. The lists explain very
little of this unit's variance (about 0.2% on eval): most of its activity is diffuse and is
not tied to any word, or to a short window of words, that we could find.
"""

READS = ()

LIMIT = {
    "expensive", "costly", "cost", "price", "afford", "pricey", "difficult", "difficulty",
    "hard", "harder", "hardest", "tough", "challenging", "complicated", "complex", "impossible",
    "unlikely", "rare", "rarely", "scarce", "limited", "unavailable", "inaccessible", "beyond",
    "cumbersome", "obscure", "slow", "slower", "require", "requires", "requiring", "readily",
    "overly", "intensive",
}
CONTRAST = {"however", "but", "although", "though", "yet", "whereas", "但", "但是", "然而", "しかし"}
REFUSE = {"cannot", "unable", "sorry", "unfortunately", "apologize", "refuse"}

LIMIT_WEIGHT, CONTRAST_WEIGHT, REFUSE_WEIGHT = 0.3, 0.4, -0.2


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in LIMIT:
        value = LIMIT_WEIGHT
    elif word in CONTRAST:
        value = CONTRAST_WEIGHT
    elif word in REFUSE:
        value = REFUSE_WEIGHT
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 194: no readable token rule found; predicts 0.

What this component is: one rank-one piece of the MLP output projection in layer 15.
It reads a direction of the MLP's hidden state and writes a fixed direction into the
residual stream. Its activation is that read-out times the write vector's norm.

What was measured (on training rows and the eval scoring):
- It is essentially never used by the model: its causal importance is about 1e-7 on
  average and it never passes the 0.1 threshold on 10M harvested tokens. Switching it
  off changes the next-token distribution by about 1e-6 nats per position.
- Its activation is roughly symmetric around 0 with std about 0.29, and it is not
  explained by anything visible in the token stream: token identity, previous token,
  position in the row, document, and broad character classes (digits, punctuation, CJK,
  capitals, whitespace) each explain under 1% of its variance on held-out rows.
- Its value is correlated from one position to the next (lag-1 autocorrelation about 0.34),
  so it tracks some slowly changing context state inside the network, not a surface pattern.

So the honest program is the null one: predict 0 everywhere. It explains essentially
none of the component's variance (about 0), and switching it off is what the
model's own output already sees.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # No token-level rule explains this component's activation, so predict 0 at every position.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 195 (down_proj component 195), predicted from context.

Plain-language reading: this unit is mildly negative on ordinary function words
(the, of, from, at, between, along, ...) when the text is a geometry or
math-problem passage, and about +0.06 everywhere else. The program keeps a
running "geometry context" score in the carry: it rises with each geometry word
(triangle, circle, vertex, angle, ...) and decays by 0.9 per token, reset at each
document boundary. On a function word, the prediction is pulled down in
proportion to that score.

This captures only the tilt of the component, not its large swings: its strongest
negative values (around -3, on about 0.2% of tokens) sit on such function words inside
geometry text, and depend on context these short word lists do not see. A lookup of
each token's mean activation explains about 3% of its variance on training rows; this
program explains about 0.3% on eval rows (a constant explains none).
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN = 0.064
DECAY = 0.9
PULL = 0.3

GEOMETRY_WORDS = frozenset(
    """triangle triangles circle circles radius radii chord chords tangent angle angles
    bisector centroid midpoint altitude perpendicular polygon rectangle pyramid sphere
    spheres cube diagonal vertex vertices parallel intersect intersects intersection
    hypotenuse perimeter segment segments plane planes point points line lines distance
    area volume edges edge side sides length coordinates""".split()
)
FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    "the of to from at on in between along a an each for per over through by with is are".split()
)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    score, doc = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != doc:
        score, doc = 0.0, prefix.document_ids[-1]
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    score = DECAY * score + (1.0 if word in GEOMETRY_WORDS else 0.0)
    value = MEAN
    if word in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        value -= PULL * min(score, 1.0)
    return (score, doc), value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 196 (this component reads almost only that unit).

What it does: it is strongly negative on the word that opens a comparison, the
'more', 'less', 'as', 'so', 'same', 'such' ... of 'X is more than Y', 'were so ...',
'as big as', and most strongly when that word follows a copula or 'with' ('is more',
'was so', 'were more'). It is near zero on fixed phrases where the word is not opening a
comparison: 'such as', 'as well as', ', as'. It is positive on two recurring contexts:
the 'Posts' label of a forum profile ('Joined: ... Posts: 5') and the shell command 'cd'.
Everything else is predicted as 0.

This covers only the comparative and these two contexts. Most of the component's variance
is a diffuse spread of small positive and negative values that no short rule captures.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that open a comparison ("more than", "as ... as", "so ... that", "less than").
DEGREE = {"more", "less", "as", "so", "same", "much", "many", "fewer", "higher", "lower",
          "better", "worse", "larger", "smaller", "greater", "plus"}
# Words that come right before a predicate ("is more", "were so", "with more").
COPULA = {"is", "are", "was", "were", "be", "been", "being", "am", "with"}
# Words before which a degree word is a fixed phrase, not a comparison ("such as", ", as").
IDIOM = {",", "such", "well", "and", "or", "just", "even"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest token."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if word == "Posts":  # forum profile line: "Joined: 02 Sep 2009 / Posts: 5"
        return None, 12.0
    if word == "cd":  # shell command
        return None, 5.0
    if word not in DEGREE or prev in IDIOM:
        return None, 0.0
    return None, (-5.0 if prev in COPULA else -1.0)

"""Predict a constant: the component's average activation.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:197 is one rank-one piece of layer 15's
MLP down projection. Its input direction is mostly MLP hidden unit 197 (about 0.24 of the
direction's weight, with unit 5336 at -0.16); its output direction is a diffuse 2048-dim
vector whose logit lens shows no clear token group.

Its activation is a dense, roughly symmetric signal (mean 0.02, std 0.31) that does not
follow any simple surface feature we could find: the current token's identity explains about
4% of its variance, script, whitespace, punctuation, repetition and distance-to-previous-
occurrence explain about 0%. So this program does not model the component; it predicts the
component's typical value everywhere, which leaves the model's next-token output almost
unchanged.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.019  # average over 65,536 training rows (about 33.5M tokens)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The same value at every position, whatever the prefix."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15, MLP hidden unit 198 (the component's activation is this unit's value).

The component is one rank-one piece of the MLP down projection that is almost entirely
hidden unit 198: its input direction is 0.85 on that unit and its output is that unit's
write into the residual stream. The unit sits near zero (median about 0.05) and is
almost always quiet. Its large values are rare, and they are negative.

This program names the few contexts where the negative spikes are easy to see:
- gratitude: "for" right after "Thanks" / "Thank you" (about -6 there), and other
  tokens within two words of "thank(s)" (about -1.3);
- printf-style format strings: the conversion letter after a "%", as in "%d" or
  "%s" (about -4).
Everywhere else it predicts 0. These rules explain well under 1% of the unit's
variance: most of its variance is spread over contexts no short rule captures.
"""

READS = ()

THANK_WORDS = ("thank", "thanks")
FORMAT_LETTERS = ("d", "s", "f", "x", "i", "u", "c", "p", "o")


def _word(text):
    return text.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position

    def back(k):
        # The token k places back, if it is in this document; otherwise ""
        i = t - k
        if i < 0 or docs[i] != docs[t]:
            return ""
        return tokens[i]

    current = _word(tokens[t])
    if _word(back(1)) in THANK_WORDS or _word(back(2)) in THANK_WORDS:
        return carry, (-6.0 if current == "for" else -1.3)
    if back(1).endswith("%") and current in FORMAT_LETTERS:
        return carry, -4.0
    return carry, 0.0

"""Romance and Arabic word endings inside dense Romance/Arabic passages.

Plain-terms summary. This component is silent in most text (English, code, numbers,
German, Russian...). It switches on in passages written in Romance languages (Spanish,
Portuguese, French, Italian, Romanian) or in Arabic and Persian script. It is strongest
on the ending of a word that the tokenizer split into several pieces, when the word is a
noun or plural in that language (-ción, -ção, -ité, -amento, -os, -ات, ...). Its sign is
mostly positive; endings typical of English or verbs (-er, -ar, -nt, -in) stay near zero.

How the program works:
  1. A word is "Romance/Arabic" if its best-matching language, among those and English
     (by word frequency, wordfreq), is one of those languages.
  2. Density: the share of the previous 20 tokens that belong to such words. Below 30%
     the component is taken as off (0). At or above 30% the passage counts as dense.
  3. In a dense passage, at the current token:
       - a word completed from 2+ pieces, ending in an abstract-noun suffix: 8
       - ... ending in an Arabic/Persian plural or feminine suffix: 7
       - ... ending in a Romance plural suffix (-os, -as, -es, -ios, ...): 5
       - ... other ending in a vowel or -s: 2.4; ending in a consonant: 1.2
       - a single-token Romance/Arabic word: 2.0 right after an article or preposition
         (un, la, el, des, de...), otherwise 0.6
     Any other token: 0.

Measured on training rows: variance explained by the activation about 10% (r about 0.33).
The simple version without the density gate explains about 5%.
"""

import regex
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

READS = ()

LANGS = ("es", "pt", "fr", "it", "ro", "ar", "fa")
WINDOW = 20
DENSE = 0.3
ARTICLES = ("un", "une", "el", "la", "los", "las", "le", "les", "des", "de", "del", "di")

ABSTRACT = regex.compile(
    r"(ción|ciones|ção|ções|ões|zione|zioni|amento|imento|ité|ités|idad|idade"
    r"|ateur|ateurs|ência|encias|ance|ances|agem|ança|ità|ione|ioni)$"
)
ARABIC = regex.compile(r"(ات|ية|ّة|های|ها)$")
PLURAL = regex.compile(r"(os|as|es|ios|ias|tos|cas|ais|aux|ils)$")
VOWEL_OR_S = regex.compile(r"[aeiousáéíóúàèìòùâêôãõ]$")

VALUE = {
    "abstract": 8.0,
    "arabic": 7.0,
    "plural": 5.0,
    "other_vowel": 2.4,
    "other_consonant": 1.2,
    "whole": 0.6,
    "whole_after_article": 2.0,
}


def _letters(b):
    """True for a token that is (part of) letters, with no space or punctuation."""
    return len(b) > 0 and all(c >= 0x80 or chr(c).isalpha() for c in b)


def _is_romance(word):
    """True if the word's best-matching language is one of LANGS, not English."""
    best = max(LANGS + ("en",), key=lambda lang: zipf_frequency(word, lang))
    return best in LANGS and zipf_frequency(word, best) >= 3


def _kind(word):
    """The kind of ending of a word completed from several pieces."""
    if ABSTRACT.search(word):
        return "abstract"
    if ARABIC.search(word):
        return "arabic"
    if PLURAL.search(word):
        return "plural"
    return "other_vowel" if VOWEL_OR_S.search(word) else "other_consonant"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    token = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        word, pieces, flags = b"", 0, ()
    else:
        word, pieces, flags = carry[1], carry[2], carry[3]

    # The token before this one, if it is in the same document.
    previous = b""
    if len(prefix.token_bytes) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == doc:
        previous = prefix.token_bytes[-2].strip().lower().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

    # Romance/Arabic share of the last WINDOW tokens of this document.
    dense = sum(flags) / WINDOW >= DENSE

    # Track the word being spelled: a token with a leading space starts a word,
    # a letter token without one continues it.
    stripped = token.lstrip(b" ")
    if token[:1] == b" ":
        word, pieces = stripped, (1 if _letters(stripped) else 0)
    elif _letters(stripped):
        word, pieces = (word + stripped if pieces > 0 else stripped), pieces + 1
    else:
        word, pieces = b"", 0

    flag, value = 0, 0.0
    if _letters(stripped):
        text = word.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").lower()
        if _is_romance(text):
            flag = 1
            if dense:
                if pieces >= 2:
                    value = VALUE[_kind(text)]
                elif previous in ARTICLES:
                    value = VALUE["whole_after_article"]
                else:
                    value = VALUE["whole"]
    flags = (flags + (flag,))[-WINDOW:]
    return (doc, word, pieces, flags), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 202: a "content word" detector that fades with distance.

The component reads the layer-15 MLP hidden state and writes a fixed direction into the
residual stream; its activation is the size of that write. Read from the token text alone,
it is:
- large on content words (a whole word after a space: nouns, adjectives, names, months),
  and somewhat smaller on word pieces that continue a word with no space;
- small on closed-class function words (the, of, and, is, not ...), on closing brackets,
  quotes and commas, and on chat or markup tags such as <|im_end|>, which go slightly
  negative;
- zero at the first token of each document, and about 0.24 lower for every doubling of
  the distance from the document's start.

The program keeps only the document position (a count reset at each new document) and the
newest token's kind. It does not look at attention or at any earlier activation.
Its values are the mean activation of each kind, fitted by least squares on training text.
It explains about 14% of the variance (r = 0.38) of the component's activation; a
token-identity table would explain about 17%, so the rest is context this program does not
see.
"""

import math
import re

READS = ()

FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    """a an the of to in on at by for with from as into about over under and or but nor so
    if then than that this these those is are was were be been being am do does did have
    has had not no it its he she they we you i me him her them us my your his our their who
    which what when where why how can could will would shall should may might must there
    here all any some each every both either neither up down out off just also only very
    more most much many such own same other""".split()
)

KIND_VALUE = {
    "content": 5.9,  # a whole word after a space: nouns, adjectives, names
    "glued": 4.7,  # a word piece with no leading space
    "function": 2.9,  # closed-class words: the, of, and, is, not ...
    "non_latin": 4.6,  # characters outside ASCII
    "punct": 3.8,  # other punctuation and symbols
    "close": 2.7,  # closing brackets, quotes, commas, semicolons
    "digit": 2.8,
    "space": 3.4,  # whitespace and newlines
    "special": 1.9,  # chat and markup tags such as <|im_end|>
}
DECAY = 0.24  # the activation falls by this much per doubling of distance into the document


def kind(text):
    """The kind of one token, from its text alone."""
    word = text.strip()
    if re.match(r"</?[|a-z_]", text):
        return "special"
    if not word:
        return "space"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]+", word):
        if word.lower() in FUNCTION_WORDS:
            return "function"
        return "content" if text.startswith(" ") else "glued"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+", word):
        return "digit"
    if re.match(r"\s*[)\]}>;:,\"'`]", text):
        return "close"
    if re.search(r"[^\x00-\x7f]", text):
        return "non_latin"
    return "punct"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label, position within the document) at the previous token.
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != document:
        position = 0  # first token of a document: the component is off there
    else:
        position = carry[1] + 1
    if position == 0:
        value = 0.0
    else:
        value = KIND_VALUE[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])] - DECAY * math.log2(position)
    return (document, position), value

"""Glued-joiner feature of layers.15.mlp.down_proj:203.

The component fires on a punctuation token that is glued onto the word before it,
with no space between them. Examples: a hyphen inside a compound (spin-fields, pull-quote),
a slash in a path or URL (src/format), an underscore or `=` in code (_Dep, x=),
an apostrophe or curly quote starting a contraction ('s, ’re). The strength depends on
the symbol: joiners that tie a word to the next piece are strongest, sentence punctuation
is weaker, and closing brackets and quotes are near zero. A hyphen or slash that follows
a digit (dates, ranges, versions like 2019-08) is weaker. Two more cases: a tab that
starts an indented line of code, and the Chinese particle 的.
Everything else, including ordinary spaced words, predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()

# Typical activation for a glued token, by the symbol it starts with.
JOINER = {
    "-": 7.0, "/": 5.8, "’": 4.8, "_": 4.0, "*": 3.7, "(": 3.2, "=": 3.1,
    "'": 3.1, "[": 2.8, "%": 2.8, "{": 2.7, "<": 2.1, ".": 2.2, "+": 1.7,
    "!": 1.5, ":": 1.3, ",": 1.1, "?": 1.0, ")": 0.1, "]": 0.2, '"': -0.2,
}
AFTER_DIGIT = {"-": 3.8, "/": 4.3}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if len(prefix.token_strings) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    if "的" in tok:
        return carry, 4.0
    if tok.startswith("\t"):
        return carry, 3.0
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    glued = bool(prev) and (prev[-1].isalnum() or prev[-1] in ")]")
    if not tok or tok[0].isspace() or not glued:
        return carry, 0.0
    if prev[-1].isdigit() and tok[0] in AFTER_DIGIT:
        return carry, AFTER_DIGIT[tok[0]]
    return carry, JOINER.get(tok[0], 0.0)

"""Negation words.

This component writes a "negation" signal into the residual stream. It responds to the
token that expresses a negation or an absence: English "not", "no", "never", "nothing",
"without", the prefixes "non-" and "un-", the contraction "n't", and the same idea in
other languages ("nicht", "sans", "без", Chinese 不 没 未 非). Those tokens get a strong
activation (about 3.5). Weaker words that set up a contrast or exclusion ("than",
"before", "instead", "beyond", "less", "lack", "avoid", "hardly") get about 1.8. The
token right after a negation word gets a small bump (about 0.85). Every other token gets 0.
Token identity is the main cue; the rest of the context explains little more.
"""

READS = ()

NEGATORS = {
    " not", " Not", " NOT", "not", "Not", "NOT", " no", " No", "no", "No", " non", " Non",
    "non", "Non", "_non", "_no", "_not", " never", "Never", "never", " nothing", " Nothing",
    "nothing", "Nothing", " without", " Without", "without", " cannot", "'t", "’t",
    " un", " Un", "un", " unc", " unp", " unb", " unm", " unre", " unf",
    " nicht", " niet", " nie", " sans", " без", " не", " ohne",
    "不", "没", "没有", "沒", "沒有", "未", "非", "不是", "无", "不用", "不需要", "不會",
}
CONTRAST = {
    " than", " before", " instead", " beyond", " less", " lack", " avoid", " neither",
    " hardly", " absent", " besides", " outside", " regardless",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Activation at the newest token, from its word and the word before it."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if word in NEGATORS:
        return carry, 3.5
    if word in CONTRAST:
        return carry, 1.8
    if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2] in NEGATORS:
        return carry, 0.85
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 209 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:209), read as a
"colon and translation-gloss" detector.

What the component does, as far as a short program can tell:
- Its value is dominated by one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (unit 209). That unit's sign and
  size depend on the surrounding text in ways no short rule captures, so most of the
  component's variance is diffuse and this program does not explain it.
- It responds most to the colon that opens a gloss in another language, as in
  "Calbayog (Waray: Syudad san Calbayog)" or "Vygodskis (Lithuanian: Jokūbas ...)":
  there it is strongly positive. The words of that gloss are mildly negative.
- Any other colon is weakly positive.

The program is a small state machine over the document's recent text:
- GLOSS_OPEN: +12.4 on the colon right after "(<language name>:".

APOSTROPHE = "'"
TOOL_END_TAGS = frozenset(["</tool_response>", "</tool_call>"])
WINDOW = 16  # tokens looked back over, within the same document

DIGIT = 0.026

and spaces. Within symbols it is larger when:
  - the symbol stands apart from a preceding word (after a space, a newline,
    another symbol, or the start of a document), not glued to a word like `foo(`;
  - it is new to its document, not a repeat of something already printed;
  - it opens a line (follows a newline), where a new separator or bullet starts;
  - it is a run of one repeated character (`---`, `===`).

and whether the previous token ended a line or a word. It predicts:

    symbol standing apart, new                     ->  2.5    (repeat: 1.2)
    ... and it opens a line                        ->  +2.9
    ... and it is a run of one repeated character  ->  +0.8

rows, rounded. Its activation also depends on context the tokens do not show
(which the program leaves out), so most of the variance is not explained.

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

GLUED_NEW, GLUED_OLD = 0.65, 0.2
APART_NEW, APART_OLD = 2.5, 1.2
LINE_START = 2.9
REPEATED_RUN = 0.8


def is_symbol(text: str) -> bool:
    """A token that is only punctuation or symbols: no letters, digits or spaces."""
    s = text.strip()
    return bool(s) and not any(c.isalnum() or c.isspace() for c in s)


def is_run(text: str) -> bool:
    """One symbol repeated: '---', '===', '____', '//'."""
    s = text.strip()
    return len(s) > 1 and len(set(s)) == 1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        seen, after_newline, after_word = set(), False, False  # a new document starts
    else:
        _, seen, after_newline, after_word = carry
    token, text = prefix.token_ids[-1], prefix.token_strings[-1]
    novel = token not in seen
    seen.add(token)

    value = 0.0
    if is_symbol(text):
        if after_word:  # glued to the word before it
            value = GLUED_NEW if novel else GLUED_OLD
        else:  # stands apart
            value = APART_NEW if novel else APART_OLD
            if after_newline and novel:
                value += LINE_START
        if is_run(text):
            value += REPEATED_RUN

    stripped = text.rstrip()
    ends_word = bool(stripped) and stripped[-1].isalnum()
    return (doc, seen, "\n" in text, ends_word), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 224: a copy-detector that pushes negative.

What it does: the component's activation is usually near zero, but goes clearly
negative when the text being read is a copy of earlier text in the same document.
The longer the run of most recent tokens that repeats an earlier run (same tokens,
same order, inside the same document), the more negative the activation. A token
seen once before gives about -0.18; a copied run of 4 gives about -0.5, and 8 about
-0.7. Most of the strongest dips (below -3) fall on copied text.

The program tracks, token by token, every earlier position that the current text
matches and how far back that match goes. Its prediction is
    -0.8 * (1 - exp(-copy_len / 4)),
where copy_len is the longest such run ending at the current token, counting the
current token. Document boundaries reset everything, as the model does.

What it does not capture: the large spread that remains at each copy length (the
component also depends on context the program does not read, and its positive
values, mostly on new text, are not explained). Variance explained on the eval rows
is about 4% (Pearson r about 0.2), so this is a weak description of the component's
sign and of its strongest dips, not a full account of its values.
"""

import math
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

SATURATION = 4.0
SCALE = 0.8


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    tok = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "tokens": [], "occurrences": {}, "runs": {}}
    tokens = carry["tokens"]
    occurrences = carry["occurrences"]
    i = len(tokens)  # local position within this document
    # runs: earlier end position j -> length of the run ending at j that matches
    # the text ending at i-1. Extend each by one token if the next token agrees.
    runs = {}
    for j, length in carry["runs"].items():
        if tokens[j + 1] == tok:
            runs[j + 1] = length + 1
    # a new run of length 1 starts at every earlier position holding this token
    for j in occurrences.get(tok, ()):
        runs[j] = max(runs.get(j, 0), 1)
    copy_len = max(runs.values(), default=0)
    occurrences.setdefault(tok, []).append(i)
    tokens.append(tok)
    carry["runs"] = runs
    value = -SCALE * (1.0 - math.exp(-copy_len / SATURATION))
    return carry, value

... digit of "1992", "3.10.19", "Col 11". A number's first digit, and every non-digit token,
stays near 0. A continuing digit starts at about 4 and is weakened in three ways:
  - it is halved when the same two-token pair already occurred earlier in the document
    (the digits are being copied, not produced);
  - it is halved again when the digit before it is 0 or 9;
  - it shrinks by a fifth for each further digit deeper into the number.

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

DIGITS = frozenset("0123456789")
BASE = 4.0  # a fresh second digit of a number
WEAK_PREVIOUS = frozenset("09")  # previous digits that weaken the next digit
DECAY = 0.8  # factor per digit beyond the second


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    ids, docs = prefix.token_ids, prefix.document_ids
    new_document = len(docs) < 2 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]
    if carry is None or new_document:
        carry = {"pairs": set(), "run": 0}  # token pairs seen in this document; digit run length
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(ids) > 1 else ""
    carry["run"] = carry["run"] + 1 if cur in DIGITS else 0
    value = 0.0

        value = BASE * DECAY ** (carry["run"] - 2)
        if (prev, cur) in carry["pairs"]:
            value /= 2
        if prev in WEAK_PREVIOUS:
            value /= 2
    carry["pairs"].add((prev, cur))
    return carry, value

Plain version: the component is positive on a word that can be a verb when the
word before it makes a verb the expected next word, such as "to", a modal
("can", "will"), "not", or a subject pronoun ("they", "we"). The same word after
an article or "of"-type word, where a noun is expected, is near zero. Words that
are only verbs in WordNet get more than words that are both verb and noun.
Everything else is near the component's average, a little below zero for
function words.

of the variance; most of the activation depends on context this table cannot see.
"""

import re

import wordnet

READS = ()

FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    "a an the of and or but to in on at by for with from as is are was were be been "
    "being it its this that these those he she they we you i me him her them us my your "
    "our their his not no do does did have has had will would can could should may might "
    "must shall than then there here what which who whom whose when where why how if so "
    "because while about into over under up down out".split()
)
# Words after which a verb is expected: infinitive "to", modals, negation, subject pronouns.
VERB_CUES = frozenset(
    "to can will would must should could may might shall cannot not never also "
    "i you we they he she it".split()
)
# Words after which a noun is expected.
NOUN_CUES = frozenset("a an the this that these those my your our their his its".split())

VERB_ONLY, VERB_NOUN = 0.45, 0.17
CUED, OTHER_FUNCTION, OTHER = 2.0, -0.03, 0.06  # multiplier after a verb cue


def word_so_far(strings):
    """The word the newest token completes: pieces back to the last word start."""
    word = ""
    for piece in reversed(strings):
        word = piece + word
        if piece[:1] in (" ", "\n", "\t") or not piece[:1].isalnum():
            break
    return word.strip().lower()


def verb_strength(word):
    """0 for non-verbs, VERB_ONLY, or VERB_NOUN for words WordNet lists as a verb."""
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", word) or word in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        return 0.0
    pos = set(wordnet.parts_of_speech(word))
    for base in wordnet.base_forms(word):
        pos |= set(wordnet.parts_of_speech(base))
    if "verb" not in pos:
        return 0.0
    return VERB_ONLY if "noun" not in pos else VERB_NOUN


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    strings = prefix.token_strings
    piece = strings[-1]
    if piece[:1].isalnum() and piece[:1] not in (" ", "\n", "\t"):

    word = word_so_far(strings)
    prev = strings[-2].strip().lower() if len(strings) > 1 else ""
    strength = verb_strength(word)
    if strength == 0.0:
        return carry, OTHER_FUNCTION if word in FUNCTION_WORDS else OTHER
    if prev in VERB_CUES:
        return carry, strength * CUED
    if prev in NOUN_CUES:
        return carry, 0.0  # a noun slot: the word is probably a noun here
    return carry, strength

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 235, read through its one decomposed component.

The component reads almost only MLP hidden unit 235 of layer 15 (its input direction is that
unit), so its activation tracks that unit. The unit is a loose detector for modern
JavaScript / TypeScript / React source code. It runs high on JS and React vocabulary
(const, export, import, useState, React, Props, className, =>), on JSX and object-literal
punctuation ({, =, ?:), and on tab indentation inside code blocks. It runs low on idioms of
other languages (C/C++, Python, Go: #include, None, NULL, :=, !=, else, require) and on
Windows line endings. It stays high or low for a while after such tokens, so the program
keeps a decaying average of the same three signals over the document so far, reset at each
new document.

The prediction is a weighted sum: the current token's three signals, and their averages.
Its weights were fitted by least squares on about 4 million positions of training text.
This is a coarse explanation. It captures only a few percent of the variance: most of the
unit's activity depends on context that no token list describes.
"""

import re

READS = ()

JS_WORDS = frozenset(
    "const export import from default async await function React Props props className "
    "useState useEffect useCallback useContext useRef interface Promise Route Mock Plugin "
    "Params Options Config Context Provider Ref State Root Menu Query filter utils react".split()
)
JS_PUNCT = frozenset(["=>", "({", "={", "?:", "=>\n", "({\n", "={(", "{...", "};\n", "./", "/utils"])
OTHER_WORDS = frozenset(":= null NULL None != == else require #include #endif .h iostream sys np".split())
DECAY = 0.97


def signals(text):
    """The three signals of one token: JS-ish, other-language-ish, and indentation."""
    word = text.strip()
    js = word in JS_WORDS or word in JS_PUNCT or re.fullmatch(r"use[A-Z]\w*", word) is not None
    other = word in OTHER_WORDS or text.endswith("\r\n")
    indent = re.fullmatch(r"\t+|[ \t]*\t[ \t]*| {4,}", text) is not None
    return (float(js), float(other), float(indent))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0))  # a new document starts with no context
    _, avg = carry
    js, other, indent = signals(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    value = (
        -0.04
        + 0.85 * js
        - 0.64 * other
        + 0.76 * indent
        + 10.4 * avg[0]
        - 2.1 * avg[1]
        + 1.8 * avg[2]
    )
    avg = tuple(DECAY * m + (1 - DECAY) * s for m, s in zip(avg, (js, other, indent)))
    return (doc, avg), value

What it does, in plain terms: it reads "we are multiplying / scaling / taking a ratio".
Its output direction, read through the unembedding, promotes words such as "ratio",
"multiplication", "reciprocal", "multiplying", "denominator" and "factor", and suppresses
"subtract", "offset" and "attr". So it is positive where a multiplicative relation is being
written (a factor, a product, times, a ratio, a multiplication sign) and negative in
additive or logarithmic contexts.

This program is a word-level approximation of that. It gives:
  * a scaling word (factor, product, times, multiply, ratio, denominator, x, cdot, ...)
    a high value after an article or "by"/"of"/a number ("a factor", "by a factor",
    "4 times"), and a lower value otherwise; "how many times" (a count) gets 0;
  * "of" right after a scaling word ("a factor of") a high value;
  * a small positive value on "=" and on a space that follows an operator (the space
    before a computed number);
  * a small negative value on logarithm / exponent / dimension / degree words.
Everything else is 0. It resets at each document boundary.

It explains only a small part of the activation: its variance explained on eval is about
1%. The activation is mostly a diffuse signal with rare large spikes that depend on
longer math context, which these word rules do not capture.

SCALE_WORDS = {
    "factor", "factors", "product", "times", "multiply", "multiplied", "multiplying",
    "multiplication", "ratio", "ratios", "denominator", "numerator", "divide", "divided",
    "dividing", "reciprocal", "fold", "doubled", "doubling", "twice", "×", "∏", "cdot",
}
# What comes before a scaling word when it is used as a multiplier: "a factor", "by 3 times".
SCALE_CUES = {"a", "an", "the", "by", "of", "each", "their", "x", "×", "hundred"}
# Operators; a space after one of these comes right before a computed number.
OPERATORS = {"=", "×", "*", "/", "÷", "cdot", "divided", "times", "multiply", "product",

# Additive or logarithmic words, where the component is weakly negative.
LOG_WORDS = {"log", "logarithm", "exponent", "exponential", "dimension", "degree", "modulus"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if word in SCALE_WORDS:

        return carry, 4.0 if prev in SCALE_CUES else 1.0
    if word == "of" and prev in SCALE_WORDS:  # "a factor of", "a product of"

    if word in LOG_WORDS:

    if word == "=":

        return carry, 0.4
    return carry, 0.0

    "week", "weeks", "day", "days", "time", "times", "ago", "past", "when", "then",
    "later", "before", "after", "since", "until", "during", "hour", "hours", "era",
    "age", "today", "earlier", "now", "while",
}

    "september", "october", "november", "december",
}

    return len(text) == 1 and text in "0123456789"

    """True when the newest token is the fourth digit of a four-digit number in one document."""
    if len(strings) < 4 or not all(is_digit(s) for s in strings[-4:]):

"""Technical-science vocabulary detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 252.

What it does: this component reads "we are inside a technical science text" (biochemistry,
molecular biology, chemistry, physics, lab methods) and fires on the technical words of such
text. Ordinary prose, code, chat and lists sit near 0 (the program predicts 0 there; the real
component dips negative in some of them, which this program does not capture). It rises to
2 to 6 on words like "receptor", "lipid", "phosphorylation", "sodium", "sulfur", "serum",
"electron", "10 mg/ml" or "μm".

How the program predicts it:
  1. Spot each technical word as it is typed (the letters ending at the current token) and
     check it against short word lists: biomedical terms, chemical elements and compounds,
     physics terms, and measurement units.
  2. Keep a running density of those words in the current document: a decaying average with
     about a 100-token memory, reset at each new document. Dense technical text means the
     component is on across the whole passage, not only at the technical word.
  3. Predict a saturating function of that density, plus a bonus on the technical word itself.

What it gets and what a table would add: on the eval rows it explains about 11% of the
activation's variance (Pearson r about 0.35). Edited into the model, its next-token KL is about
85% of what switching the component off does, and its cross-entropy effect is slightly
beneficial, where switching it off is slightly harmful. On training text, a per-token table
of average activations with the same running density reached about 0.18 of variance
(out of sample); these word lists give most of that and read as a concept a reader can check.
"""

import math

import regex

READS = ()

BIOMED = frozenset(
    """
    cell cells protein proteins gene genes genetic genome enzyme enzymes receptor receptors
    tumor tumour tumors cancer carcinoma lymphoma leukemia infection infections infected virus
    viruses viral bacteria bacterial antibody antibodies antigen immune immunity lipid lipids
    cholesterol plasma serum blood liver kidney muscle tissue tissues brain neuron neurons
    neuronal cortex mice mouse rats rat patient patients clinical disease diseases therapy
    therapies drug drugs dose expression mrna dna rna chromosome chromatin mutation mutations
    apoptosis apoptotic autophagy oxidative oxidation peroxidation insulin hormone hormones
    estrogen cytokine cytokines inflammation inflammatory activation activated phosphorylation
    kinase ligand membrane mitochondrial mitochondria metabolism metabolic enzymatic peptide
    molecular molecule molecules compound compounds acid acids oxide plasmid pathway pathways
    binding induced induction inhibitors inhibitor residues amino polymer glucose cellular
    ldl ifn pcr buffer extracted immunoblot macrophage endothelial lymph epithelial strains
    variants nuclear replication transcription signaling signal nucleus cytoplasm phosphate
    atp promoter dimer igg sds pbs gaba
    """.split()
)

CHEMISTRY = frozenset(
    """
    hydrogen helium lithium beryllium boron carbon nitrogen oxygen fluorine neon sodium
    magnesium aluminum aluminium silicon phosphorus sulfur sulphur chlorine argon potassium
    calcium titanium vanadium chromium manganese iron cobalt nickel copper zinc arsenic
    selenium bromine iodine molybdenum silver cadmium platinum mercury uranium thorium cesium
    barium ethanol methanol ethyl acetone benzene chloride nitrate sulfate hydroxide carbonate
    solvent ion ions thermal electron electrons spectral density
    """.split()
)

PHYSICS_AND_UNITS = frozenset(
    """
    neutron photon phonon quark absorption scattering polarization excitation
    mg ml mm μm um nm μl ul hz khz mhz kda mmol bp
    """.split()
)

TERMS = BIOMED | CHEMISTRY | PHYSICS_AND_UNITS

DECAY = 0.99  # per token: the density's memory is about 100 tokens
TAU = 0.05  # density at which the saturating curve has reached 63% of its height
HEIGHT = 4.1  # the saturating part's top, in activation units
OWN_BONUS = 1.2  # extra for a technical word itself


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    density, word = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, "")
    if len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        density, word = 0.0, ""  # a new document: forget the topic and the word
    # The letters ending at this token (the word typed so far), as the text reads.
    word = regex.search(r"\p{L}+$", word + prefix.token_strings[-1])
    word = word.group(0).lower() if word else ""
    own = 1.0 if word in TERMS else 0.0
    value = HEIGHT * (1 - math.exp(-density / TAU)) + OWN_BONUS * own
    density = DECAY * density + (1 - DECAY) * own
    return (density, word), float(value)

"""Word-unfinished detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 253.

What the component does (from measurements on training rows): it is mostly quiet,
but when the text so far ends in the middle of a word, i.e. the current token is an
unfinished piece of a longer word (`vocab|ulary`, `Södert|örns`, `neg|otiated`), it
turns strongly negative. Its strongest negative values come on such pieces when the
next token continues the same word. Token identity alone predicts nothing, and
neither does the current token's script: it is the word-so-far that matters.

This program reads the current word-so-far (the run of letters ending at this token,
restarted at each non-letter and each document start), and looks it up in a
multilingual word list (wordfreq's top 100k words in 30 languages):
  - the word-so-far is an unfinished prefix of a listed word (and not a listed word
    itself): predict -1.25, the typical size of the component's negative spikes there;
  - otherwise (a complete listed word, an unknown word, or no word-so-far): 0.
"""

import bisect

import regex
from wordfreq import top_n_list

READS = ()

LANGS = [
    "en", "de", "fr", "es", "it", "pt", "nl", "sv", "pl", "ru", "tr", "id", "fi",
    "da", "no", "cs", "hu", "ro", "el", "ar", "uk", "vi", "sk", "hr", "sl", "lv",
    "lt", "ca", "eu",
]
WORD_SET = set()
for lang in LANGS:
    WORD_SET.update(w.lower() for w in top_n_list(lang, 100000))
WORDS = sorted(WORD_SET)

UNFINISHED = -1.25  # word so far is a proper prefix of a listed word


def is_unfinished(word):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(WORDS, word)
    return i < len(WORDS) and WORDS[i].startswith(word)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = carry or ""
    pos = prefix.position
    if pos > 0 and prefix.document_ids[pos] != prefix.document_ids[pos - 1]:
        word = ""
    text = prefix.token_bytes[pos].decode("utf-8", "ignore")
    run = regex.search(r"\p{L}+$", text)
    if run is None:
        word = ""
    elif run.group(0) == text:
        word = word + text
    else:
        word = run.group(0)
    w = word.lower()
    if not w:
        value = 0.0
    elif w not in WORD_SET and is_unfinished(w):
        value = UNFINISHED
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return word, value
